items.reference:
🧪 Correctness testing asks

does this do what it's supposed to, for the inputs I expect?

🕵️ Security asks

what can this do if someone deliberately sends inputs I didn't expect, meaning to misuse it?
items.learnMore:
Correctness vs. security

Two different questions asked of the same code, with two different test suites.

CorrectnessSecurity
QuestionDoes it work?Can it be misused?
Inputs testedExpected / validDeliberately adversarial
Passing tells youThe happy path worksNothing about the unhappy paths

Common mistake

Treating 'all tests pass' as evidence of security. A green test suite only covers the inputs someone thought to write a test for.
items.prompt: A checkout function passes every functional test: correct totals, correct tax, correct discounts, for all the inputs QA tried. What does this tell you about whether it's secure?
choices: It proves the function is secure, since it handles every case correctly
Nothing directly — functional tests check the intended/expected inputs, not what happens under deliberately malicious or unexpected input
It proves the function is secure against every attack except SQL injection
Security and correctness are the same property, so passing one implies the other
items.explanation: Correctness testing answers 'does this work for the inputs I expect' — security asks 'what happens for inputs an adversary deliberately chooses.' These are different questions with different test suites; passing one says nothing about the other, which is exactly why 'it works' and 'it's safe' can diverge.

items.prompt: A code reviewer says 'this looks fine, the tests are green' about a new API endpoint. What question has that reviewer not yet asked?
choices: Whether the code follows the team's style guide
What an adversary — not a normal user — could make this endpoint do if they sent it input nobody expected
Whether the tests run fast enough in CI
Whether the endpoint has enough code comments
items.explanation: Green tests confirm the intended behavior for the inputs someone thought to test. The security mindset is a separate, additional question: what happens under input chosen specifically to break the intended behavior — that question isn't answered by the test suite passing.

items.prompt: Why can a system be 'working' (all features function as specified) and still be unsafe?
choices: Because 'working' is a marketing term with no technical meaning
Because 'working' only confirms the paths the designer intended function correctly — it says nothing about paths nobody intended, which is exactly where adversaries operate
Because all software has bugs, so 'working' is never really true
It can't — a fully working system is always safe by definition
items.explanation: Functional correctness is scoped to the intended behavior. Security failures live in the gap between 'what the designer thought about' and 'what's actually reachable' — a system can satisfy every intended requirement and still expose an unintended one.

items.reference:
🌐 Untrusted

user browsers, third-party APIs, file uploads — anything outside your control

🔒 Trusted

your own services, once their inputs have already been validated

Why: every crossing from untrusted to trusted is a place assumptions must be re-earned.
items.learnMore:
Trust boundaries

The line between 'controlled by us' and 'controlled by someone else' is where re-validation has to happen.

SideExampleAssumption you can make
UntrustedUser input, webhook payload, uploaded fileNone — could be anything
TrustedYour own database, your own internal cacheAlready validated once, by you

Common mistake

Assuming a value is safe because it 'came from the database' without checking how it got into the database in the first place — if it entered via an untrusted path and was never validated, storing it doesn't retroactively make it trustworthy.
items.prompt: A field called `isAdmin` arrives as part of a JSON body sent directly from a user's browser. Should the server trust its value?
choices: Yes — if the client sent it, the server can assume it's accurate
No — the browser is outside the system's control, so any value it sends has crossed a trust boundary and must be independently verified, not taken at face value
Only if the request uses HTTPS
Yes, as long as the JSON parses without errors
items.explanation: Anything a client can set, a client can lie about. `isAdmin` coming from the browser is exactly the kind of value that crossed a trust boundary — well-formed JSON says nothing about whether the claim inside it is true.

items.prompt: Why does a value moving from your API server to your own internal cache generally need less re-validation than a value arriving from a user's browser?
choices: Caches are inherently more secure than databases
The API-to-cache path only carries data your own system already produced or already validated — nothing new is being trusted, unlike a value an outside party controls
There's no real difference — every data movement needs identical scrutiny
Internal traffic is always encrypted, so it's automatically safe
items.explanation: A trust boundary marks where control changes hands. Server-to-cache traffic (assuming both are yours) never leaves your control, so nothing new needs to be re-earned — the browser-to-server path does, because the browser is fully outside your control.

items.reference:
🙋 Normal review

does this do what it's supposed to?

🕵️ Adversarial review

how would I break this, on purpose?
items.learnMore:
The security mindset as a reflex

A one-word change to the question a reviewer asks, applied as a default, not a special pass.

ReviewerQuestion askedFinds
FunctionalIf a user does X, is the result correct?Broken features
Security-mindedIf an adversary does X on purpose, is the result still safe?Exploitable gaps the functional question can't see

Common mistake

Treating adversarial thinking as a separate, occasional activity done by a security team, rather than a default habit applied during normal design and code review.
items.prompt: What is the 'security mindset' as described in this unit?
choices: Memorizing a list of known vulnerabilities and checking code against it
Actively asking 'how would I break this' as a normal part of reviewing any design, instead of only asking 'does this work'
Refusing to ship any feature that touches user input
A specialized skill only security engineers need, not general engineers
items.explanation: The mindset is a reflex, not a checklist: habitually asking the adversarial question alongside the functional one. It doesn't require memorizing every specific vulnerability — that's what structured tools like STRIDE and later units are for.

items.prompt: Why doesn't the security mindset come naturally during normal engineering work?
choices: Because most engineers are careless by nature
Because normal engineering practice is optimized for the happy path — building and verifying that the intended behavior works — which is a different exercise than deliberately imagining misuse
Because security is only relevant to a small number of specialized companies
Because it requires knowledge of cryptography most engineers don't have
items.explanation: Day-to-day engineering optimizes for 'does the intended thing happen' — writing the feature, testing the feature, shipping the feature. Adversarial thinking requires a deliberate shift to 'what if this were used against its intent,' which nothing about writing the happy path prompts you to do automatically.

items.reference:
Spoofing
Tampering
Repudiation
Info disclosure
Denial of service
Elevation of privilege

Why: six distinct lenses for 'what could go wrong,' not six specific bugs.
items.learnMore:
STRIDE, letter by letter

Each letter names a category of adversary goal, not a specific vulnerability.

LetterCategoryAdversary's goal
SSpoofingPretend to be someone/something else
TTamperingAlter data or code in transit or at rest
RRepudiationDeny having done something, with no proof
IInformation disclosureRead data they shouldn't have access to
DDenial of serviceMake the system unavailable to legitimate use
EElevation of privilegeGain access beyond what was granted

Common mistake

Memorizing the six words without the underlying question each one asks — STRIDE is only useful as a set of prompts you actively run through per component, not a term to recite.
items.prompt: What does the 'T' in STRIDE stand for, and what adversary goal does it describe?
choices: Trust — verifying a user is trustworthy
Tampering — altering data or code in transit or at rest
Testing — running functional tests against the system
Timeout — causing requests to expire
items.explanation: Tampering is the STRIDE category for altering data or code — for example modifying a price value in a request before it reaches the server, or changing a file's contents after it's stored.

items.explanation: Elevation of privilege is specifically about a caller ending up with more access than intended — a regular user reaching an admin-only endpoint is the canonical example.

items.reference:
Threat modeling happens before a design is built, not after it breaks.

✅ Before code

cheap to change: a design conversation

🔥 After an incident

expensive to change: a rework, a postmortem, a rebuild
items.learnMore:
Why timing matters

The same architectural mistake costs wildly different amounts depending on when it's caught.

When caughtCost to fixWhat's already sunk
During designA conversation, maybe a redraw of a diagramNothing yet
During code reviewA changed function, before mergeOne PR's worth of code
After an incidentAn architecture rework, a postmortem, user trustShipped code, real users, real damage

Common mistake

Treating 'think like an adversary' as a checklist run by a separate team right before launch — by then, fixing a trust-boundary mistake often means reworking the architecture, not patching a line.
items.prompt: When should threat modeling for a new component ideally happen?
choices: After the component has shipped, as part of an incident postmortem
Before the component is built, as part of the design — the same way you'd sanity-check an architecture, not as a late-stage gate
Only if the component handles payment data
Threat modeling is only useful for legacy systems, not new ones
items.explanation: Threat modeling is meant to happen during design, before the code exists — catching a trust-boundary mistake at the whiteboard stage costs a conversation; catching the same mistake after launch can mean reworking the architecture.

items.prompt: A team treats security review as a checklist a separate team runs right before launch. What's the risk in that approach?
choices: There is no risk — as long as the checklist eventually runs, timing doesn't matter

By the time the checklist runs, the design itself was never adversarially examined — fixing a fundamental trust-boundary mistake at that point often means reworking the architecture, not patching a line
Checklists are inherently less thorough than a design conversation
This approach is fine only for internal tools, not customer-facing ones
items.explanation: A late-stage-only security pass means the architecture itself was designed without the adversarial question ever being asked. Anything found that late is expensive to fix precisely because the design already committed to a shape that assumed it wouldn't be needed.

items.reference:
🤖 Automated attacks

scanners probing millions of hosts for a known pattern — don't care how small or unknown you are

🎯 Targeted attacks

a person specifically choosing your company — obscurity does reduce this
items.learnMore:
"We're too small to be targeted"

Obscurity reduces the odds of a targeted attack, not an automated one.

Attack typeWho initiates itDoes obscurity help?
Automated / untargetedA script scanning for a known vulnerable pattern across the internetNo — the scanner doesn't know or care who you are
TargetedA person specifically choosing your companySomewhat — smaller/unknown targets are less likely to be chosen

Common mistake

Assuming low profile equals low risk. Most real-world exploitation of small or obscure systems is automated, not the result of someone specifically hunting that company.
items.prompt: A small startup's engineer argues 'we don't need to threat model, we're too small and unknown for anyone to bother attacking us.' What's the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: There's no flaw — small companies are never worth attacking

Most real-world exploitation of small or obscure systems is automated and untargeted (scanners probing for a known vulnerable pattern across millions of hosts); obscurity reduces the odds of a targeted attack, not an automated one
Small companies are actually more attractive to attackers than large ones
This is only a flaw for companies that handle payment data
items.explanation: An automated scanner finds vulnerable patterns by scanning broadly, not by researching which companies are 'worth' attacking. Being small or unknown lowers the odds of a targeted attack but does nothing against a script that would find the same bug in your system as in a Fortune 500's.

items.prompt: The tampering bug from this unit (a checkout endpoint that trusts a client-supplied price) is more likely to be found by which of the following?
choices: A person who specifically researched the company and targeted it
An automated scanner or script trying common tampering patterns against many sites, with no idea which company it hit
Nobody — this class of bug is too obscure to be found in practice
Only a professional penetration tester hired by the company itself
items.explanation: Trusting a client-supplied price is a common, well-known pattern — exactly the kind of thing automated tooling checks for at scale, with no need for anyone to have specifically targeted the company first.

Repudiation
Info disclosure
Denial of service
Elevation of privilege

Why: each real scenario maps to exactly one adversary goal.
items.learnMore:
Matching a real scenario to a STRIDE category

The trick is naming the adversary's goal, not the technical mechanism.

ScenarioAdversary's goalCategory
Bypassing a hidden admin button by calling the endpoint directlyGain access beyond what was grantedElevation of privilege
A stack trace in an error page reveals internal file pathsRead data they shouldn't haveInformation disclosure
Sending oversized payloads to exhaust server memoryMake the system unavailableDenial of service
Forging a header to look like an internal servicePretend to be someone elseSpoofing

Common mistake

Categorizing by the technical mechanism (e.g. 'this is an HTTP header issue') instead of the adversary's actual goal — the same mechanism can serve different goals in different scenarios.
items.prompt: A user discovers that if they call an admin-only API endpoint directly (bypassing the UI, which just hides the button), it works even though they're not an admin. Which STRIDE category is this?
choices: Repudiation
Denial of service
Elevation of privilege
Information disclosure
items.explanation: This is elevation of privilege — gaining access beyond what was actually granted. Hiding a button in the UI is not an authorization check; the server-side endpoint has to independently verify the caller is allowed to perform the action, regardless of what the client interface shows.

items.explanation: Leaking data the requester shouldn't have access to — internals like file paths, connection strings, or stack traces — is information disclosure. Even without directly compromising anything, this hands an attacker reconnaissance detail that makes other attacks easier.

choices: Spoofing
Tampering

items.explanation: Pretending to be someone or something else — here, forging identity via a header — is exactly spoofing. It's distinct from tampering (altering data) and elevation of privilege (gaining access beyond a grant), even though a spoofing attack often leads to one of those as a follow-on effect.

items.reference:
Untrusted: user browser, third-party webhook → API server (trust boundary) → trusted: database, internal cache

Why: a crossing means the system must actively decide whether to believe what it's receiving.
items.learnMore:
Reading a trust-boundary diagram

Every arrow crossing from untrusted to trusted is a decision point, not just a data path.

ArrowCrosses a trust boundary?What has to happen
User browser → API serverYesRe-validate every assumption about the data
Third-party webhook → API serverYesVerify sender, verify payload, don't assume good faith
API server → internal database (already-validated write)NoNothing new to trust — it's data you already own

Common mistake

Assuming every arrow in a system diagram needs identical scrutiny. Only crossings from a zone you don't control into one you do require re-earning trust.
items.prompt: In a trust-boundary diagram, why does a value crossing from the user's browser into the API server need to be re-validated, while a value moving from the API server to its own internal cache doesn't (to the same degree)?
choices: The internal cache is slower, so extra validation there would hurt performance
The browser is outside the system's control — an adversary can send anything through it — while the API-to-cache path only carries data the system itself already produced or validated
There's no real difference; every data movement needs identical validation
Because HTTP requests are inherently less secure than internal function calls
items.explanation: A trust boundary marks the line between 'controlled by us' and 'controlled by someone else.' Data crossing into the system from an untrusted source needs its assumptions re-earned; data moving between components you already control and already validated doesn't carry the same risk, because nothing new is being trusted.

items.prompt: A system diagram shows a third-party webhook sending payloads directly into an API server. What does marking this arrow as crossing a trust boundary actually require the API server to do?
choices: Nothing extra — third parties are generally trustworthy business partners
Independently verify the payload's origin and contents, the same way it would for any other untrusted input, rather than assuming the third party's claims are accurate
Reject all webhook traffic outright
Only log the payload for later review, without validating it
items.explanation: A third party is outside your control even if you have a business relationship with them — their system could be compromised, or the payload could be forged in transit. Crossing a trust boundary means actively verifying, not assuming good faith because of who claims to be sending it.

items.reference: STRIDE is six lenses to look through per component — not a fixed list of bugs to search for.
items.learnMore:
STRIDE as lenses, not a bug list

Running all six questions against a component surfaces categories a functional review structurally can't reach.

ApproachQuestion askedWhat it can find
Functional reviewDoes the intended flow work?Broken features
STRIDE run per componentCould someone spoof/tamper/repudiate/etc. here?Categories of risk the functional review never asks about

Common mistake

Treating STRIDE as a specific list of six bugs to search for, rather than six recurring questions to re-ask for every new component — the six categories are prompts, not a checklist item you can 'complete' once.
items.prompt: Is STRIDE best understood as a checklist of six specific bugs to search for?
choices: Yes — once all six specific bugs are ruled out, the component is secure
No — it's a set of six lenses (categories of adversary goal) to run through per component, surfacing risk categories a purely functional review wouldn't think to ask about
STRIDE only applies to network-facing components, not internal ones
Yes, and it's exhaustive — nothing outside the six categories is worth considering
items.explanation: STRIDE's value is in the questions, not a fixed inventory of bugs. For any component, asking 'could someone spoof a caller here? Tamper with this data? Deny they did this?' surfaces categories a functional review (which only asks 'does the intended flow work') is structurally blind to.

items.prompt: A team runs STRIDE once on a component at launch and considers the analysis permanently 'done.' What's the risk in that?
choices: None — STRIDE only needs to be run once per component, ever
The component's design, dependencies, and entry points can change over time; STRIDE is a lens to re-apply as a component evolves, not a one-time certificate that stays valid forever
STRIDE analysis becomes more accurate the longer it's left unrevisited
This is only a risk for components that handle payment data
items.explanation: STRIDE's six questions are a recurring habit, not a one-time stamp of approval — a component that grows new entry points, new dependencies, or new trust boundaries needs the same six questions re-asked against its new shape.

items.reference: Threat modeling produces a ranked list (likelihood × impact) — not an attempt to eliminate every conceivable risk.
items.learnMore:
Ranking, not eliminating

The goal is knowing where mitigation effort pays off most, the same way you'd triage bugs by severity.

ApproachGoalRealistic?
Eliminate all conceivable riskZero riskNo — impossible for any real system
Rank by likelihood × impactHighest-value mitigation effort spent firstYes — this is what threat modeling actually produces

Common mistake

Treating an unranked, exhaustive list of every conceivable threat as the deliverable — without prioritization, a team has no way to decide where to actually spend limited mitigation effort.
items.prompt: What's the actual output of a threat-modeling exercise, per the `threat_model()` procedure in this unit?
choices: A list of threats sorted alphabetically by component name
A ranked list of threats, ordered by likelihood times impact, so the highest-priority risks get mitigation effort first
A single yes/no verdict on whether the system is 'secure'
An exhaustive list of every conceivable risk, with no prioritization
items.explanation: Threat modeling deliberately produces a ranked, not exhaustive, list — the point isn't eliminating all conceivable risk (impossible) but knowing where the highest-value mitigation effort should go, the same way bugs get triaged by severity rather than fixed in file-alphabetical order.

items.prompt: Why does threat modeling rank threats by likelihood × impact instead of just listing every plausible threat with no order?
choices: Because likelihood and impact are the only two properties threats can have
Because mitigation effort is limited, and an unranked list gives no guidance on which risks are actually worth addressing first
Ranking is only necessary for very large systems
Because impact alone is always a sufficient ranking signal, likelihood doesn't matter
items.explanation: A team has finite time and engineering effort. A ranked list (likelihood × impact) tells you which risks are worth fixing first — an unranked list of every plausible threat provides no such guidance and risks spending effort on low-value fixes while high-value ones wait.

items.reference:
📝 Repudiation

denying an action happened, with no proof to contradict the denial

Mitigation: an audit log that records who did what, when.
items.learnMore:
Repudiation and audit trails

The defense against repudiation is a record, not a policy.

SituationCan the action be attributed?STRIDE category
Admin action with no audit logNo — anyone with access could have done it, unprovablyRepudiation
Admin action logged with actor, timestamp, actionYes — there's a record to point toMitigated

Common mistake

Assuming that because an action requires authentication, it's automatically attributable later — authentication proves who acted at the time, but without a persisted log, there's nothing to prove it after the fact.
items.prompt: An admin can delete any user's account, but the system keeps no record of which admin performed a given deletion. Which STRIDE category does this gap fall under?
choices: Tampering
Repudiation
Spoofing
Denial of service
items.explanation: Repudiation is about being able to deny having done something, with no proof to contradict the denial. Without an audit log recording who performed the deletion, no admin's denial can be disproven — even if the deletion is otherwise fully authorized and functioning correctly.

Admin action with no audit logNo — anyone with access could have done it, unprovablyRepudiation
Admin action logged with actor, timestamp, actionYes — there's a record to point toMitigated

Common mistake

Assuming that because an action requires authentication, it's automatically attributable later — authentication proves who acted at the time, but without a persisted log, there's nothing to prove it after the fact.
items.prompt: What's the standard mitigation for the repudiation STRIDE category?
choices: Rate limiting the sensitive action
An audit log that records who performed an action and when, so a denial can be checked against a record
Encrypting the action's data at rest
Requiring two-factor authentication for the action
items.explanation: Repudiation is specifically about the absence of proof — the fix is a persisted record (an audit log with actor, timestamp, and action) that lets a later dispute be checked against real evidence, not just against whatever the person currently claims.

items.reference:
🐘 Denial of service

making the system unavailable to legitimate use, not by breaking in but by exhausting a resource
items.learnMore:
Recognizing denial-of-service risk

The adversary doesn't need to compromise anything — just exhaust a shared resource.

ExampleResource exhausted
Oversized payloads sent repeatedlyServer memory
No rate limit on a login endpointCPU / database connections
Unbounded file uploadsDisk / storage quota

Common mistake

Only thinking of denial of service as a large-scale, coordinated attack — an endpoint with no size or rate limit can be knocked over by a single script, no coordination required.
items.prompt: An endpoint accepts file uploads with no maximum size limit and no per-user rate limit. What STRIDE category does this expose the system to?
choices: Spoofing
Information disclosure
Denial of service
Repudiation
items.explanation: Repeatedly uploading large files with no size or rate limit can exhaust server storage or bandwidth, making the service unavailable for legitimate users — that's denial of service, and it requires no authentication bypass or data theft to pull off.

items.prompt: Why is 'no rate limit on a public endpoint' specifically a denial-of-service concern?
choices: Because it always leads to a data breach
Because an adversary can call it as fast as automation allows, exhausting shared resources (CPU, memory, connections) until the system can't serve legitimate requests
Because rate limits are only relevant for authentication endpoints
It isn't a real concern unless the endpoint modifies data
items.explanation: Without a rate limit, nothing stops an adversary from calling the endpoint as fast as their tooling allows — enough repeated calls exhaust a shared resource (CPU, memory, connection pool), degrading or breaking service for everyone else, which is exactly the denial-of-service goal.

items.reference:
📏 Shape validation

is it a number? is it in range? — confirms the input is well-formed

🔐 Trust validation

should this value be believed at all for this purpose?
items.learnMore:
Shape validation vs. trust validation

A well-formed value and a trustworthy value are different properties.

CheckConfirmsCatches the price-tampering bug?
price is a positive number under 10,000ShapeNo — 0.01 passes this check
price is recomputed server-side from the catalogTrustYes — the client's value never influences the result

Common mistake

Adding more validation rules (range checks, type checks) to a value that shouldn't have been trusted as an input at all — the fix for a trust-boundary problem is architectural, not another regex.
items.prompt: A field `price` in a checkout request is validated to be a positive number under 10,000. Does this validation prevent the tampering bug from L3 (client sending price: 0.01 for a $40 item)?
choices: Yes — 0.01 would fail the positive-number check
No — 0.01 is a valid positive number under 10,000, so shape validation doesn't catch it; the actual fix is not trusting a client-supplied price for a security-sensitive calculation at all
Yes, but only if combined with rate limiting
The question is unanswerable without knowing the currency
items.explanation: Shape validation (is it a number, is it in a plausible range) confirms the input is well-formed — it doesn't confirm the input should be trusted for this purpose. The real fix is architectural: recompute price server-side from data the client never controls, not add more validation rules to a value that shouldn't cross the trust boundary as an input in the first place.

items.prompt: A discount-code field is validated with a regex ensuring it's 6 uppercase letters. Does this shape check tell you anything about whether the discount percentage it unlocks should be trusted from the client?
choices: Yes — a well-formed code is automatically a legitimate one
No — the regex only confirms the code's format, not whether the discount amount tied to it was correctly looked up server-side rather than trusted from the client
Yes, but only for codes shorter than 6 characters
Shape validation is irrelevant to discount codes specifically
items.explanation: Format validation and trust validation answer different questions. A 6-letter uppercase string can still be paired, client-side, with a forged discount percentage — the fix is looking up the real discount server-side from the code, the same pattern as the price fix, not just checking the code's shape.

items.reference: A file-upload endpoint, run through all six STRIDE categories, surfaces six distinct real risks a functional spec ("accepts an image, saves it") never mentions.
items.learnMore:
Running STRIDE against a boring feature

Even an ordinary feature has a mitigation per category, once you ask.

CategoryRisk on a file-upload endpointMitigation
TamperingUploaded file is something other than an image, disguised by extensionVerify actual file content (magic bytes), not just the extension
Information disclosureUpload path leaks internal storage structure or other users' filesStore under a random, user-scoped key, never the client-supplied filename
Elevation of privilegeThe 'image' is actually an executable script that gets served and runServe from a separate domain/bucket with no execute permissions

Common mistake

Checking only the file extension and assuming that confirms the file's actual content — an attacker fully controls both the extension and the bytes inside the file.
items.prompt: On the file-upload endpoint from this unit, why is checking only the filename extension (e.g. must end in .jpg) an insufficient mitigation for the Tampering category?
choices: It isn't insufficient — extension checks are a complete mitigation

The extension is just a string the client fully controls; a file's actual bytes can be anything regardless of what its name claims, so the mitigation has to verify content (magic bytes), not the filename
Extension checks only matter for the Denial-of-service category, not Tampering
Because .jpg files can never contain malicious content, regardless of validation
items.explanation: A filename's extension is metadata the client sets — it says nothing about the actual bytes inside the file. Verifying real content (checking magic bytes, the actual byte signature of a known file format) is what closes the gap an extension-only check leaves wide open.

items.prompt: Why does storing an uploaded file under the client-supplied filename risk Information disclosure, specifically?
choices: It doesn't — filenames have no security relevance
A predictable or attacker-chosen filename can let one user guess or overwrite another user's file, or reveal internal storage layout — using a random, user-scoped key removes that guessable structure
This is actually a Denial-of-service risk, not Information disclosure
Only if the filename is longer than 255 characters
items.explanation: A client-controlled, predictable filename can expose or collide with another user's stored file, or reveal how storage is organized internally — replacing it with a random, user-scoped key removes the attacker's ability to guess or target another user's files.

items.reference: The fix: never let a client-supplied value determine a security-sensitive result. Recompute from server-side data instead.
items.learnMore:
Removing an untrusted value's ability to matter

The mitigation isn't filtering the bad value — it's never giving it a code path to influence the result.

VersionSource of truth for priceTamperable?
VulnerablecartItem.price (client-supplied)Yes
Fixedcatalog[productId].price (server-side)No — client has no path to influence it

Common mistake

Trying to 'sanitize' or clamp the client-supplied value instead of removing its ability to matter entirely — a clamp still trusts the value's shape, which isn't the actual problem.
items.prompt: Implement `checkoutTotal(cartItem, catalog)`, the fixed version from L3: it must compute the charge using ONLY the server-side `catalog` (an object mapping productId to `{ price }`), never any `price` field that might be present on `cartItem` itself — the whole point is making a client-supplied price impossible to use, not just ignored by convention.

tests.description: computes the correct total from the catalog price
ignores a tampered client-supplied price entirely
a different quantity scales correctly

items.explanation: The fix reads `price` from `catalog[productId]` and never touches `cartItem.price` at all — not filtering it out, just never giving it a code path that could influence the result. That's the actual mitigation for a trust-boundary crossing: remove the untrusted value's ability to matter, rather than trying to sanitize a value that shouldn't be trusted for this purpose regardless of its shape.

items.reference: The fix: never let a client-supplied value determine a security-sensitive result. Recompute from server-side data instead.
items.learnMore:
Removing an untrusted value's ability to matter

The mitigation isn't filtering the bad value — it's never giving it a code path to influence the result.

VersionSource of truth for priceTamperable?
VulnerablecartItem.price (client-supplied)Yes
Fixedcatalog[productId].price (server-side)No — client has no path to influence it

Common mistake

Trying to 'sanitize' or clamp the client-supplied value instead of removing its ability to matter entirely — a clamp still trusts the value's shape, which isn't the actual problem.
items.prompt: Implement `checkoutTotalWithShipping(cartItem, catalog, shippingRates)`. It must compute `product.price * quantity + shippingRates[cartItem.shippingMethod]`, using ONLY `catalog` for price and ONLY `shippingRates` for the shipping cost — `cartItem` may carry client-supplied `price` and/or `shippingCost` fields that must never be read, the same trust-boundary rule as the plain checkout function, now applied to two values instead of one.

tests.description: computes price + shipping from server-side sources
tests.expr: expect(checkoutTotalWithShipping({ productId: 'sku-1', quantity: 1, shippingMethod: 'standard' }, { 'sku-1': { price: 20 } }, { standard: 5 })).toEqual(25)

tests.description: ignores a tampered client-supplied price
tests.expr: expect(checkoutTotalWithShipping({ productId: 'sku-1', quantity: 1, shippingMethod: 'standard', price: 0.01 }, { 'sku-1': { price: 20 } }, { standard: 5 })).toEqual(25)

tests.description: ignores a tampered client-supplied shippingCost
tests.expr: expect(checkoutTotalWithShipping({ productId: 'sku-1', quantity: 1, shippingMethod: 'express', shippingCost: 0 }, { 'sku-1': { price: 20 } }, { express: 15 })).toEqual(35)

items.explanation: Both security-sensitive values — price and shipping cost — are read exclusively from server-side sources (`catalog`, `shippingRates`), keyed by client-supplied identifiers (`productId`, `shippingMethod`) that only select *which* server value to use, never *what* the value is. The client can pick which product or shipping method, but never what either one costs.

items.reference: A filename's extension is a claim; a file's magic bytes are evidence. Check the evidence.
items.learnMore:
Magic bytes

Most binary file formats start with a fixed byte signature that identifies the format, independent of filename.

FormatFirst bytes (hex)
PNG89 50 4E 47
JPEGFF D8 FF

Common mistake

Checking the Content-Type header sent by the client instead of the file's actual bytes — the header is just as client-controlled as the filename extension.
items.prompt: Implement `isPng(bytes)` where `bytes` is a `Uint8Array` of a file's first bytes. Return `true` only if the file starts with the PNG magic-byte signature `0x89 0x50 0x4E 0x47`, regardless of what any filename or Content-Type claims.

tests.description: recognizes a real PNG signature
rejects a file claiming to be PNG by name but with different bytes
rejects a too-short buffer

items.explanation: The function checks the file's actual first bytes against PNG's fixed signature, entirely independent of any filename or claimed Content-Type — this is what a real content-validation mitigation for the Tampering category looks like: verify the evidence (bytes), not the claim (name/header).

items.prompt: Implement `isJpeg(bytes)` where `bytes` is a `Uint8Array`. Return `true` only if the file starts with the JPEG magic-byte signature `0xFF 0xD8 0xFF`.

tests.description: recognizes a real JPEG signature
rejects a PNG's bytes even if named .jpg
rejects an empty buffer

items.explanation: Same principle as PNG detection, applied to JPEG's own fixed signature: the check reads the actual bytes the file starts with, which an attacker controls only by controlling the real file content — unlike a filename or Content-Type, which can be set to anything with no relationship to the bytes.

items.reference: Mitigating Denial of service: cap how many actions a caller can perform in a window, before the resource gets exhausted.
items.learnMore:
Fixed-window rate limiting

The simplest rate limiter: count calls per key within a time window, reject once the cap is hit.

ConceptRole
keyIdentifies the caller (user id, IP, API key)
windowThe time span a count applies to
limitMax allowed calls per key, per window

Common mistake

Rate limiting globally instead of per-key — a global limit lets one abusive caller exhaust the entire allowance and block every legitimate user, not just themselves.
items.prompt: Implement `createRateLimiter(limit)` returning a function `allow(key)` that returns `true` for a call if `key` has been called fewer than `limit` times so far (across the lifetime of the limiter — no time window needed for this simplified version), and `false` once `key` hits the limit. Each key is tracked independently.

tests.description: allows calls under the limit
denies once the limit is hit
tests.expr: const allow = createRateLimiter(2); allow('user1'); allow('user1'); expect(allow('user1')).toBe(false);

tests.description: tracks each key independently

items.explanation: A `Map` keyed per-caller tracks each key's own count independently, so one caller hitting their limit never affects another caller's allowance — the mitigation is specifically about capping a shared resource per identity, not globally, which is what keeps a single abusive caller from starving everyone else.

items.reference: Mitigating Denial of service: cap how many actions a caller can perform in a window, before the resource gets exhausted.
items.learnMore:

ConceptRole

windowThe time span a count applies to

items.prompt: Implement `createSizeLimiter(maxBytes)` returning a function `allow(sizeInBytes)` that returns `true` if `sizeInBytes` is less than or equal to `maxBytes`, and `false` otherwise — this is the size-limit half of Denial-of-service mitigation for an upload endpoint, independent of the count-based rate limiter.

tests.description: allows a file at exactly the limit
rejects a file over the limit
allows a small file

items.explanation: Denial-of-service mitigation for uploads typically needs both a per-caller count limit (the rate limiter) and a per-request size limit (this function) — an attacker who can send unlimited count but is capped in size, or unlimited size but capped in count, is still bounded on the dimension that was actually enforced.

items.reference: Mitigating Repudiation: every sensitive action gets a permanent, attributable record — actor, action, timestamp.
items.learnMore:
Append-only audit logging

The log's value comes from being complete and attributable, not from being clever.

FieldWhy it's required
actorWho performed the action — the whole point, for repudiation
actionWhat was done
timestampWhen — needed to reconstruct a sequence of events

Common mistake

Logging only 'an admin deleted a user' without recording which admin — a log that can't attribute an action to a specific actor doesn't actually mitigate repudiation, it just documents that something happened.
items.prompt: Implement `createAuditLog()` returning an object with `record(actor, action, timestamp)` (pushes an entry `{ actor, action, timestamp }`) and `entriesFor(actor)` (returns an array of all entries recorded for that actor, in the order they were recorded).

tests.description: records an entry and retrieves it by actor
tests.expr: const log = createAuditLog(); log.record('alice', 'delete-user', 1000); expect(log.entriesFor('alice')).toEqual([{ actor: 'alice', action: 'delete-user', timestamp: 1000 }]);

tests.description: keeps different actors' entries separate
tests.expr: const log = createAuditLog(); log.record('alice', 'delete-user', 1000); log.record('bob', 'edit-user', 1001); expect(log.entriesFor('bob')).toEqual([{ actor: 'bob', action: 'edit-user', timestamp: 1001 }]);

tests.description: preserves recording order for the same actor
tests.expr: const log = createAuditLog(); log.record('alice', 'login', 1); log.record('alice', 'delete-user', 2); expect(log.entriesFor('alice').map(e => e.action)).toEqual(['login', 'delete-user']);

items.explanation: Every entry is appended, never overwritten or removed, and always carries who/what/when — that's what makes it usable as evidence against a later denial. `entriesFor` filtering by actor is what lets a specific claim ('I never did that') be checked against a specific person's real recorded history.

items.reference: Mitigating Repudiation: every sensitive action gets a permanent, attributable record — actor, action, timestamp.
items.learnMore:
Append-only audit logging

The log's value comes from being complete and attributable, not from being clever.

FieldWhy it's required
actorWho performed the action — the whole point, for repudiation
actionWhat was done
timestampWhen — needed to reconstruct a sequence of events

Common mistake

Logging only 'an admin deleted a user' without recording which admin — a log that can't attribute an action to a specific actor doesn't actually mitigate repudiation, it just documents that something happened.
items.prompt: Implement `wasActionPerformed(log, actor, action)` given a log with an `entriesFor(actor)` method (same shape as `createAuditLog()`'s return value). Return `true` if any entry for `actor` has that exact `action`, `false` otherwise — this is the actual repudiation check: 'can we prove this specific actor performed this specific action.'

tests.description: returns true when the actor has that action recorded
tests.expr: const log = { entriesFor: () => [{ actor: 'alice', action: 'delete-user', timestamp: 1 }] }; expect(wasActionPerformed(log, 'alice', 'delete-user')).toBe(true);

tests.description: returns false when the action isn't in the actor's entries
tests.expr: const log = { entriesFor: () => [{ actor: 'alice', action: 'login', timestamp: 1 }] }; expect(wasActionPerformed(log, 'alice', 'delete-user')).toBe(false);

tests.description: returns false for an actor with no entries at all

items.explanation: This is the query side of the repudiation mitigation: given a claim ('I never deleted that user'), the audit log either has a matching recorded entry for that actor or it doesn't — the entire value of append-only logging is making this a factual lookup instead of a matter of whoever's word is trusted more.

items.reference: Mitigating Elevation of privilege: the server independently checks the caller's actual role, every time, not just whether they're logged in.
items.learnMore:
Authorization independent of authentication

Being logged in proves identity; it says nothing about what that identity is allowed to do.

CheckQuestion answeredMissing it causes
AuthenticationIs this a real, logged-in session?Spoofing risk
AuthorizationIs this specific user allowed to do this specific thing?Elevation of privilege

Common mistake

Hiding an admin-only button in the UI and treating that as the security control — the server-side endpoint has to independently verify the caller's role, since a hidden button is trivially bypassed by calling the endpoint directly.
items.prompt: Implement `authorize(user, requiredRole)` where `user` is `{ id, roles }` (`roles` an array of strings). Return `true` if `user.roles` includes `requiredRole`, `false` otherwise — this is the server-side check that has to run regardless of whether a UI button is shown or hidden.

tests.description: allows a user with the required role
denies a user without the required role
denies a user with no roles at all

items.explanation: This check runs entirely server-side, off the caller's actual stored roles — it has no dependency on what the client's UI does or doesn't show, which is exactly why it closes the elevation-of-privilege gap that a merely-hidden button leaves open (a hidden button is a UI convenience, not an access control).

items.reference: Mitigating Elevation of privilege: the server independently checks the caller's actual role, every time, not just whether they're logged in.
items.learnMore:
Authorization independent of authentication

Being logged in proves identity; it says nothing about what that identity is allowed to do.

CheckQuestion answeredMissing it causes
AuthenticationIs this a real, logged-in session?Spoofing risk
AuthorizationIs this specific user allowed to do this specific thing?Elevation of privilege

Common mistake

Hiding an admin-only button in the UI and treating that as the security control — the server-side endpoint has to independently verify the caller's role, since a hidden button is trivially bypassed by calling the endpoint directly.
items.prompt: Implement `requireOwnerOrAdmin(user, resource)` where `user` is `{ id, roles }` and `resource` is `{ ownerId }`. Return `true` if `user.id === resource.ownerId` OR `user.roles` includes `'admin'`; `false` otherwise — the common pattern of 'you can edit your own resource, or an admin can edit anyone's.'

tests.description: allows the resource owner
allows an admin who isn't the owner
denies a non-owner, non-admin

items.explanation: The check is a direct, explicit OR of the two conditions that should actually grant access — ownership or an admin role — with no implicit trust of anything the client claims about itself. Missing either half of this check is a real elevation-of-privilege bug: dropping the ownership check locks owners out, dropping the admin check locks out legitimate admin overrides.
